set.statement: As summarized by a 2010 narrative review (Degenhardt, Bruno, et al., 2010), studies of people who use ecstasy have found that some meet criteria for dependence, but the share ranges from about 4 in 100 to 73 in 100 depending on who was asked, how, and over what period. In two US household surveys, 3.6 in 100 people who had used ecstasy in the past year (Wu et al.) and 3.8 in 100 of those who had started within the previous two years (Stone et al.) met criteria for hallucinogen dependence. In a German community study, 0.4 in 100 of all young adults met past-year criteria for ecstasy, hallucinogen or stimulant dependence, and 5.8 in 100 of people who had ever used ecstasy had ever met criteria (about 12 of 207 people, by our arithmetic from the table). In samples recruited differently, 19 in 100 of New York nightclub attendees and 22 in 100 of Taiwanese juvenile detainees who used ecstasy met past-year criteria, and 16 to 18 in 100 in convenience samples in Germany, the UK and Australia (195, 1,106 and 1,662 people) were counted as dependent or scored above a screening scale's cut-off. The highest figures, 43, 64 and 73 in 100 over a lifetime, came from three small samples: 52 adolescents and young adults in drug treatment and in the community who had used ecstasy at least 5 times, 185 people the review describes as regularly using ecstasy, and 59 rave attendees who had taken at least 250 tablets in their lifetime. The review says all the instruments were designed for other drugs, only one study used a clinician's assessment, assessment was mostly by self-report and lifetime recall, and most samples were recruited by convenience or snowball methods, so the figures cannot be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy; it adds that people often reported dependence symptoms despite relatively infrequent use and that it is unclear whether they understood the questions as intended, and that pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some dependence may be on another drug. Across studies, the symptoms most often reported included continued use despite problems, spending a lot of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal; in two studies the symptoms fell into a group about compulsive use and a group about escalating use (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended). In the one study that followed people (the German community study above), 93 in 100 of those who met criteria at the start no longer did just over three years later and 50 in 100 had stopped using ecstasy altogether; the review does not give the size of that group, which by our arithmetic was about 12 to 14 people. In Australia, fewer than 1 in 100 treatment episodes were for ecstasy. The review also describes animal studies in which MDMA is rewarding but may be less so than other illicit drugs, and notes a lack of case reports of severe withdrawal. It concludes that the evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is thin in scope and design.

change: Editor: in-text citations now use the APA 7 label of the reference list: Degenhardt, Bruno, et al. (2010), since a second Degenhardt et al. (2010) paper (the cross-national gateway study) joined the reference list; no change of finding.
